subject: psychology
topic: More choice can leave you less satisfied
angle: Choice overload is not a universal rule but depends on specific conditions like task difficulty, set complexity, and preference uncertainty.
title: The Myth of Choice Overload

hooks.text: When does your freedom feel like a burden?
You think more choice hurts. The evidence says otherwise.

reveal.headline: Choice overload is not a universal rule.
reveal.body: A meta-analysis of 63 conditions found a mean effect size of virtually zero for choice overload.

explain.headline: Conditions dictate your experience.
explain.body: Choice overload is significant only when tasks are difficult, sets are complex, preferences are uncertain, and you aim to minimize effort.

matters.headline: Diversity can simplify your world.
matters.body: That may be why a diverse set of items can increase your satisfaction and reduce the perceived difficulty of choosing.

example.headline: A shelf of spices.
example.body: You stand in a kitchen aisle. You look at a wall of different jars. Some are familiar. Others are new.

stat.label: mean effect size of choice overload across 63 conditions

claims.text: A meta-analysis of 63 conditions from 50 published and unpublished experiments (N=5,036) found a mean effect size of virtually zero for choice overload.
claims.quote: In a meta-analysis of 63 conditions from 50 published and unpublished experiments (N=5,036), we found a mean effect size of virtually zero but considerable variance between studies.

claims.text: More choices may instead facilitate choice and increase satisfaction.
claims.quote: A number of studies found strong instances of choice overload in the lab and in the field, but others found no such effects or found that more choices may instead facilitate choice and increase satisfaction.

claims.text: When moderating variables are taken into account the overall effect of assortment size on choice overload is significant.
claims.quote: Finally, we document that when moderating variables are taken into account the overall effect of assortment size on choice overload is significant—a finding counter to the data reported by prior meta-analytic research.

claims.text: Higher levels of decision task difficulty, greater choice set complexity, higher preference uncertainty, and a more prominent, effort‐minimizing goal facilitate choice overload.
claims.quote: We further show that each of these four factors has a reliable and significant impact on choice overload, whereby higher levels of decision task difficulty, greater choice set complexity, higher preference uncertainty, and a more prominent, effort‐minimizing goal facilitate choice overload.

claims.text: Diversification increases the perceived diversity and attractiveness of the item set, while at the same time reducing the perceived difficulty of choosing from the set.
claims.quote: Study 1a tests the effectiveness of the latent feature diversification, and shows that diversification increases the perceived diversity and attractiveness of the item set, while at the same time reducing the perceived difficulty of choosing from the set.

claims.text: Diversification can increase users’ satisfaction with the chosen option, especially when they are choosing from small, diverse item sets.
claims.quote: Study 1b subsequently shows that diversification can increase users’ satisfaction with the chosen option, especially when they are choosing from small, diverse item sets.

verdict: The evidence shows that while choice overload can occur under specific conditions, it is not a consistent effect and can sometimes be mitigated or even reversed by factors like diversification.
caveat: No sufficient conditions for choice overload could be identified in the meta-analysis of 63 conditions.
caption:
More choice does not always lead to less satisfaction.

Research shows that choice overload is not a consistent effect. While it can occur under specific conditions like high task difficulty, it is not a universal rule. No sufficient conditions for choice overload could be identified in a major meta-analysis.

Does having more options actually make your life easier?
